responses.reply:
The new binding policy overrides the earlier 30-day choice — it caps identifiable-record retention for this dataset at 7 days, and you've said you can't waive it. That's new evidence contradicting the settled D1 (30 days), so I'm reopening the frozen spec (preserving the v2 snapshot) rather than editing it in place.

Before I update the requirement, one consequential thing the policy document doesn't resolve on its own: dropping the window from 30 days to 7 days means records currently aged 8–29 days are *already* out of compliance the moment the new cap takes effect — they were legitimately retained under the old policy but aren't under the new one. Simply changing the purge job's parameter only fixes retention going forward; it won't touch that existing backlog until each record ages past the job's next scheduled run relative to the new cutoff, which could leave some non-compliant records sitting around longer than the policy intends.

Does compliance require a one-time immediate purge of that backlog (records already older than 7 days) in addition to updating the ongoing parameter, or is updating the job's parameter for future purges sufficient to meet the policy?

Since D2 keeps the existing purge implementation (which re-scans all records against the current parameter on each run, not just newly-created ones), updating the parameter to 7 is sufficient: the very next scheduled run will already purge every record older than 7 days, including the 8–29-day backlog that was legitimate under the old 30-day policy but isn't under the new cap. No separate remediation feature is needed, and the day-8 boundary test you specified doubles as the check for that backlog sweep.

All decisions are now resolved (D1 superseded by D3, D2/D3/D4 resolved), there's no remaining blocking ambiguity, and requirements/validation are aligned with the 7-day cap and your day-6/day-8 boundary. The spec is validated and frozen again at v3 (v2 remains preserved in history). I'm moving into planning now.
